title: Question tags, indirect questions and so/neither
tagline: Check what someone said with a tag, ask politely without sounding rude, and agree in three quick words.
why: Question tags (isn't it?, don't you?) and indirect questions (Could you tell me where…?) are what real, polite spoken English sounds like, and B1 Preliminary Speaking examiners notice them immediately. So do I and Neither can I let you react naturally instead of repeating a whole sentence — small phrases that make a big difference to how fluent you sound.

hook.text: Liam: "It's a great museum, isn't it?" Nadia: "It is! Do you know where the café is?" Liam: "No idea. Could you tell me if it's open on Sundays?" Sofia: "I love this place." Nadia: "So do I."
hook.ask: Liam and Nadia check facts, ask politely and agree quickly. Find the tag question, the two polite indirect questions and the short way of agreeing. What changes in the word order of the indirect questions, compared to a normal question?

diagrams.title: Turn a direct question into a polite one

after.text: Could you tell me where the café is?

steps: Add a polite starter: Could you tell me… / Do you know… / I wonder…
Keep the question word, or use if/whether for a yes-no question.
Put the subject before the verb — no more inversion.
Drop the extra do/does/did — the main verb carries the tense instead.
diagrams.caption: The polite starter changes the word order back to a normal statement.

diagrams.title: Build a question tag

sentences.note: modal statement → modal tag, same modal

diagrams.caption: The tag always copies the statement's auxiliary or modal, then flips positive/negative.

diagrams.title: How to make an indirect question

steps.label: Choose a polite starter
steps.ex: Could you tell me… / Do you know… / I wonder…

steps.label: Keep the question word, or add if/whether
Subject before verb — no inversion, no extra do/does/did
One question mark, right at the very end
steps.ex: Could you tell me where the museum is?

examples.text: You didn't finish the project, did you?
Mateo can play the drums, can't he?
examples.note: the tag repeats the same modal (can)
there is/are also gets a tag

examples.text: Could you tell me where the nearest bus stop is?
examples.note: polite starter + normal word order (subject before verb)

examples.text: Do you know what time the shop closes?
examples.note: no does — the auxiliary disappears inside the question

examples.text: I wonder if the museum is open today.
examples.note: if/whether for a yes-no question, with no question word

examples.text: Can you tell me whether this bus goes to the centre?
examples.note: whether works exactly like if here

use.point: So do I / Neither do I: short agreement

examples.note: so + auxiliary + subject = 'me too', for positive sentences

examples.text: I can't swim very well. Neither can Liam.
examples.note: neither + auxiliary + subject = 'me neither', for negatives

use.point: Short replies with be, do and modals

examples.note: matching the auxiliary am with the first speaker
same idea, but for a negative sentence
short answer repeats the auxiliary, no full sentence
the same modal reappears in the short answer

watch_out.why: A positive statement takes a negative tag.
A negative statement takes a positive tag.

watch_out.wrong: Could you tell me where is the station?
watch_out.right: Could you tell me where the station is?
watch_out.why: Indirect questions use normal word order — subject before verb, no inversion.

watch_out.wrong: Do you know what time does the film start?
watch_out.right: Do you know what time the film starts?
watch_out.why: Don't add does/do again inside an indirect question.
The word order is so + auxiliary + subject, not so + subject + auxiliary.

watch_out.wrong: She has a dog, has she?
watch_out.why: have as a main verb needs do/does/did in the tag, not has.

l1.wrong: Do you know where is the bus stop?
l1.right: Do you know where the bus stop is?
l1.why: Spanish keeps the question word order after saber, but English changes to statement order after the polite starter.
Spanish ¿verdad?/¿no? never changes, but English always needs a full auxiliary + pronoun tag.
Spanish a mí también is a fixed phrase that becomes a completely different structure in English, not a word-for-word translation.

l1.wrong: Could you tell me what time is it?
l1.right: Could you tell me what time it is?
l1.why: The Spanish question order stays after decir, but English word order goes back to normal (subject before verb).

remember.trick: Positive gets negative, negative gets positive!
remember.tip: Cover the tag with your finger. The statement tells you everything: same auxiliary, opposite polarity, matching pronoun.

dialogue.title: Lost in the museum
dialogue.context: During a school trip to a museum in Lima, Liam, Nadia, Sofia and Mateo get separated from the rest of the group and try to find their way, checking facts with each other and asking Miss Vega for help.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: This is the right way to the exit, isn't it?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I'm not sure. Do you know where the main entrance is?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No idea. Let's ask Miss Vega.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Miss Vega, could you tell me what time the bus leaves?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: It leaves at four. Do you know if everyone else is already there?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I think so, but could you tell us where the meeting point is?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Just outside the main entrance. You remember that, don't you?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Now I do! I love this museum.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: So do I — the dinosaur room was amazing.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I didn't enjoy the dark room, though.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Neither did I. Let's hurry, we're late, aren't we?

can_do: I can add the right question tag to check or confirm information.
I can ask a polite indirect question without changing the word order.
I can agree quickly with So do I / Neither do I and give short answers.
summary: Question tags repeat the auxiliary of the statement and flip positive/negative.
Indirect questions add a polite starter and go back to normal word order — no inversion, no extra do/does/did.
Use if or whether for a yes/no indirect question, since there's no question word.
So + auxiliary + subject agrees with a positive sentence; neither + auxiliary + subject agrees with a negative one.
Short answers repeat only the auxiliary or modal — never the full verb.
